## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The narrative context also relates to novice monastic training (including the qualification of being able to scare crows) and the occasion when the novice Rāhula, unable to share quarters with fully ordained monks, spent the night in the Buddha's privy [Kieffer-Pülz; Ratanamalai 2007].

Curated parallels exist across virtually all surviving Vinaya recensions, including the Sarvāstivāda (*pātayantika* 53/54), Mūlasarvāstivāda (*pācittiya* 54), Mahāsāṃghika (*pācattika* 42), Dharmaguptaka (*pācittiya* 5), and Mahīśāsaka (*pācittiya* 7) traditions in Sanskrit, Chinese, and Tibetan, as well as the corresponding bhikkhunī rule (Theravāda Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 101) [Clarke]. In text-reuse analysis, DharmaNexus identifies 816 matching passages with 152 Pali texts, most extensively with the Khandhaka literature—including the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* (Kd 16), *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* (Kd 6), and *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1)—and related Vibhaṅga rules such as Pācittiya 6 and 7 [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments are also identified in Tibetan Vinaya treatises, including the *Vinayasaṃgraha* (D4105) and the *Vinayasūtraṭīkā* (D4120) [DharmaNexus]. An English translation has been produced by Bhikkhu Brahmali.
